sections.heading: MT940 Tag Structure and What Each Field Means
paragraphs: The MT940 format organizes data into a sequence of tagged fields, beginning with a basic header statement tag that identifies the account and statement period.
Transaction lines use a dedicated tag that encodes the value date, booking date, debit or credit indicator, amount and reference in fixed positions.
An informational tag carries free-text details such as the transaction description, counterparty name and any remittance information the bank includes.
Understanding these tags helps you verify that the converted output matches what your treasury management system or accounting software expects to receive.

sections.heading: Date Formats and Currency Normalization
paragraphs: Banks commonly express dates in the six-digit format used across SWIFT messaging, while plain text sources may provide dates in various regional arrangements.
The converter normalizes date strings to the bank-standard format regardless of whether your source uses dashes, slashes or compact numeric sequences.
Currency amounts are parsed from the text and placed into the correct positional fields, handling decimal separators and thousands grouping as needed.
This normalization step eliminates the most common reason MT940 imports fail: malformed dates or amounts that do not conform to the expected layout.

sections.heading: Generating Test Fixtures for Integration Pipelines
paragraphs: Development teams building treasury integrations need realistic MT940 fixtures to test parsers, reconciliation engines and dashboard imports.
Creating those fixtures from plain text data is significantly faster than exporting them from a live bank environment, especially during early development stages.
The converter lets you iterate quickly: adjust a transaction row in the text, reconvert and feed the result into your test suite within seconds.
This rapid feedback loop catches parsing bugs before they reach production, where misclassified transactions can cause reconciliation headaches.

sections.heading: Common Validation Errors and How to Avoid Them
paragraphs: Banks reject MT940 files that have missing mandatory tags, incorrect line lengths or amounts that do not balance within a statement section.
The converter enforces field lengths and character positions automatically, preventing the majority of structural validation failures before you download the file.
If your source text is missing a required field such as the account number or statement number, the tool flags the issue during conversion rather than producing an incomplete file.
Running a validation check after conversion gives you a final confirmation that the output will pass the importer's format gate on the first submission.

sections.heading: Handling Multiple Accounts in One Conversion
paragraphs: Organizations managing several accounts often need to produce separate MT940 statements for each, even when the source text contains intermixed transactions.
The converter lets you group transactions by account identifier before generating the output, ensuring each statement file corresponds to exactly one account.
This grouping prevents the downstream reconciliation errors that occur when a single file contains mixed account data that parsers cannot separate cleanly.
Batch-friendly design means you can process multiple text excerpts sequentially without reconfiguring the layout mapping each time.
